title: Salinity imprints in the North Atlantic suggest recent circulation change
highlight_text: Since the mid-2010s, freshwater anomalies originating in the western Subpolar North Atlantic have propagated at shallow and intermediate depths toward the eastern North Atlantic and adjacent marginal seas. This lower-salinity signal originated partly from changes in the Labrador Current pathway. The signal of this freshening has weakened in recent years.       2025 marked a broadscale return to average or above-average salinity conditions across most time series, except for a few regions at the limits of the propagation pathways (e.g., mode waters in the Canary Basin and the West Greenland Current). At the same time, deeper waters of the Northeast American Shelf have shown cooling and freshening, indicating an increased contribution of Labrador Current waters relative to Gulf Stream source waters since about 2023.

title: High temperatures in the upper layers
highlight_text: Sea surface and near-surface temperatures remained warm across large parts of the North Atlantic in 2025, although not as warm as those observed in 2023 and 2024. Extremely warm sea surface temperatures (including several marine heat waves) were observed in spring (in particular April, May, and June) over parts of the Northwest European shelf and the eastern North Atlantic, and in autumn in the eastern Nordic and Barents seas (October and November).

title: Record shallow convection in the Labrador Sea
highlight_text: In early 2025, winter convection in the Labrador Sea reached its shallowest depth since measurements began in the 1930s. This is due to persistently warm conditions in the subpolar North Atlantic since 2021, combined with freshening triggered by increased Arctic sea ice loss.

title: Changing signature of the Mediterranean Sea at depth
highlight_text: Observations indicate sustained warming and salinification of the Mediterranean Outflow Water affecting intermediate Atlantic waters near the Strait of Gibraltar. This signal can be traced across the eastern margin of the Atlantic Ocean from the Bay of Biscay and the Cantabrian Sea to the Canary Basin.

title: Early signs of a strong El Niño event
highlight_text: As a preview for 2026, measurements and ocean model forecasts indicate that a strong El Niño event is developing in the tropical Pacific. Previous strong El Niño events have been associated with changes in the North Atlantic Ocean, such as extended marine heatwaves in the region and a reduction in hurricanes. The 2026/27 event is therefore likely to have a strong impact on conditions in the North Atlantic.​
